section_summary: This section covers political, ideological, and religious affairs in Japan from February to April 1938, opening with General Sadao Araki's controversial public statements regarding the Anti-Comintern Pact and reports on a major Tokyo Wartime Thought Control Exhibition designed to foment spy paranoia and anti-communist sentiment. It records the uncontested passage of the National General Mobilization Bill through the Japanese House of Representatives, as well as an unexpected anti-British address delivered by an Indian nationalist at an Osaka Rotary Club luncheon. Finally, it presents an extensive report by the American Consul General at Osaka analyzing mounting official harassment and nationalist hostility directed against Christian educational institutions and foreign missionaries, highlighted by crises at Doshisha University.

subfiles.about: Newspaper clippings transmitted with Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 2798 reporting General Sadao Araki's interview and subsequent public clarifications regarding Japan's participation in the Anti-Comintern Pact.
subfiles.summary: Concluding pages of Despatch No. 2798 with four clippings: Araki's interview and letter that Japan joined the Anti-Comintern Pact from fear of communism, and a Japan Times editorial on shared spiritual principles.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2798: Statements and Clippings on General Sadao Araki and the Anti-Comintern Pact

subfiles.about: State Department routing slip recommending examination of Embassy Tokyo's despatch concerning the Wartime Thought Control Exhibit.
subfiles.summary: Brief memo drawing attention to Grew's despatch on the Wartime Thought Control Exhibit in Tokyo, which shows how Japan conditions opinion.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Despatch on Wartime Thought Control Exhibit in Tokyo

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch analyzing the ideological implications of the Wartime Thought Control Exhibit in Tokyo, with an enclosed newspaper clipping describing the display.
subfiles.summary: Grew analyzes the Cabinet Information Bureau's Thought Control Exhibit at Takashimaya: it stokes spy mania, uses German-style anti-Semitic propaganda and presents Japan in an anti-communist crusade.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2799: Wartime Thought Control Exhibit in Tokyo

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch reporting the passage of the National General Mobilization Bill without amendment by the Japanese House of Representatives.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the House of Representatives passed the National General Mobilization Bill on March 16, 1938 unamended after parties capitulated for minor concessions; a face-saving resolution accompanied it.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2815: Mobilization Bill

subfiles.about: Department of State cross-reference sheet indexing file 894.00/781 regarding Japanese internal affairs.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet for 894.00/781; no text, date or sender inscribed.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: 894.00/781

subfiles.about: Consular report describing an unexpected anti-British address by an Indian nationalist at an Osaka Rotary Club meeting attended by the Consul General.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Makinson reports at an Osaka Rotary luncheon, Indian nationalist D. N. Sahay unexpectedly gave a thirty-minute speech denouncing Britain, embarrassing the club.
subfiles.title: Report on Osaka Rotary Club Meeting and Address by D. N. Sahay

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum assessing an incoming consular despatch on the growing pressure confronting Christianity in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Memo on an Osaka despatch: few novel facts, but concrete illustrations that Christianity faces mounting pressure in Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Osaka Despatch Concerning Christianity in Japan

subfiles.about: Consular despatch transmitting an extensive report analyzing mounting political suspicion and harassment directed against liberal Christianity and Christian schools in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Makinson transmits a comprehensive thirteen-page report entitled 'Liberal Christianity Suspect in Japan,' examining the precarious position of Christian churches, educational institutions, and foreign missionaries under wartime nationalism. The report details escalating nationalist attacks on Doshisha University in Kyoto, including disputes with military instructors, the forced resignation of President Hachiro Yuasa over trivial incidents, the arrest and interrogation of his prospective successor Dr. Nishio for misquoting an imperial poem, and negotiations with the Ministry of Education to incorporate the Imperial Rescript on Education into the university charter. It further reviews the forced departure of American missionary Frank Cary from Hokkaido, police surveillance of foreign teachers in Wakayama and Kyoto, and notes that the Roman Catholic Church has largely escaped harassment due to the Vatican's conciliatory policy toward Japan and the Anti-Comintern Pact.
subfiles.title: Despatch Enclosing Report 'Liberal Christianity Suspect in Japan'
